lesson.title: Inside the Routing Table: Where a Router Keeps What It Has Learned
lesson.summary: A routing table is a router's master record of every destination network it knows how to reach, including the next hop, the cost, and how that route was learned.
lesson.body:
If routing is the ongoing process of figuring out good paths through a network, the routing table is where the results of that process live. Every router maintains one: a list of destination networks it knows about, along with, for each one, the next hop to send packets toward, the outgoing interface, a cost or metric describing how good that path is, and often a note on where the entry came from, whether an administrator typed it in by hand or a routing protocol like RIP learned it from a neighboring router.

A small routing table might look like this. For destination network 192.168.2.0/24, the next hop is 10.0.0.2, out interface eth0, at a cost of 2. For destination network 192.168.3.0/24, the next hop is also 10.0.0.2, out eth0, at a cost of 3. For 0.0.0.0/0, a special entry we will return to shortly, the next hop is 10.0.0.1, out eth1. Each row answers the same question for a different destination: if a packet needs to go here, where do I send it next, and how good is that path.

The routing table is not the same thing as the forwarding table, even though the two are closely related and sometimes blurred together in casual conversation. The routing table is deliberately descriptive: it can hold multiple candidate routes to the same destination, keep metrics around for comparison, and get rebuilt whenever the routing process learns something new. The forwarding table is derived from it, usually the single best route per destination, stripped down and optimized purely for the speed of the forwarding decision. When the routing table changes, for example because a link failed or a better path was learned, the router regenerates the relevant forwarding table entries so future packets take the new, correct path.
